introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives one definition to three things usually kept apart. Nature is “the necessary relations inherent in the realities of things.” Fate is those same relations. And religion, or divine law, is “the necessary relationships deriving from the realities of things” as a Manifestation of God perceives them. The phrase comes from Montesquieu, whose opening sentence in The Spirit of Laws is given here, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that philosophers could see that law must follow from the nature of things but could not themselves read that nature fully. The readings draw out the consequences: everything is connected, change is constant, moral law is reason and justice and no arbitrary will, and no single measure works until minds are united. Muir, Darwin, Paul and Martin Luther King speak for interdependence, Heraclitus for change, Epictetus for fate, Job for the limits of human knowledge. Hume doubts that any necessary connection can be found at all, and Hobbes holds that law is command.
questions: Nature, fate and religion are all defined as “necessary relations.” What does it mean to say that a religious law is the same kind of thing as a law of nature?
Hume says we see one event follow another and never the tie between them. If necessity cannot be observed, how is it known, in science and in ethics?
“The Laws of God are not imposition of will.” Hobbes says there is no injustice before there is a commanding power. Think of one moral rule. Which account explains it better?
If fate is the necessary relations among things, what in a human life is fated and what is open? Compare Epictetus and Khayyám.
Philosophers concluded that laws should follow from the nature of things, and the readings say that to frame such laws is “beyond human capacity.” Why would seeing the principle not be enough?

outside.why: Nature is “the essential properties and the necessary relations inherent in the realities of things,” all “closely connected together.” John Muir in the Sierra: when we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.
Darwin’s last page: an entangled bank, with plants, birds, insects and worms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner.

The relations are called necessary. Hume looked for the necessity and reported that it cannot be seen: one event follows another; but we never can observe any tie betwixt them: they seem conjoined, but never connected. What grounds the “necessary” in ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s account, if observation alone cannot?
The relationships sometimes require wakefulness and sometimes sleep, sometimes plenty and sometimes less. Ecclesiastes: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
“Until the minds of men become united, no important matter can be accomplished.” Paul: whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
Martin Luther King from the Birmingham jail: we are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.
The world “is transformed every moment and altered with every breath.” Heraclitus: an ever-living Fire, with measures of it kindling, and measures going out.

That murder, theft and falsehood are vile, “every rational mind can grasp.” Paul: the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law; these shew the work of the law written in their hearts.

“The Laws of God are not imposition of will, or of power … but the resolutions of truth, reason and justice.” Hobbes held that right and wrong begin with a power that commands: where there is no common Power, there is no Law: where no Law, no Injustice. Is a thing right because it is commanded, or commanded because it is right? What do the readings answer?

Composition and decomposition must proceed “according to the natural order … the most great law of God.” The Qur’án: thou wilt not find for Allah’s way of treatment any substitute, nor wilt thou find for Allah’s way of treatment aught of power to change.

Fate consists “in the necessary and indispensable relationships which exist in the realities of things.” Epictetus begins from the same division of the world: some things are in our control and others not.

Fate as the order of relations. FitzGerald’s Khayyám feels it as a sentence already written: the Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, moves on. Does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s definition leave more room for human action than the poet’s?

“Religion consists in the necessary relationships deriving from the realities of things.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adapts the most famous sentence of Montesquieu’s Spirit of Laws: laws, in their most general signification, are the necessary relations resulting from the nature of things.

Philosophers saw that laws must follow from the nature of things; “but … to institute such laws is beyond human capacity.” God to Job: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.

The rules and relationships are “the divine law and the social order.” Pope on what follows if one link fails: from Nature’s chain whatever link you strike, tenth or ten thousandth, breaks the chain alike.

montesquieu-necessary-relations.text: LAWS in their most general signification, are the necessary relations resulting from the nature of things
